title: Recover One Historical File
concept: Restore narrowly from a known revision

writing.summary: Restore narrowly from a known revision.
writing.rule: A one-file restore must preserve every unrelated current edit.
writing.explanation:
A rollback need not replace a whole project. To recover one file, first inspect its contents at an exact historical commit, compare it with the current file, then confirm the replacement. A full commit identity makes the preview stable while branch names continue moving.

The native git restore command opens a preview; applying the restore remains an explicit UI action. This lab models the resulting tree change: replace just the requested path from the historical tree, or remove it if it did not exist there. Preserve unrelated work and deterministic ordering. Restoring a file is also an uncommitted edit; review and commit it as a new change when it belongs in shared history. Do not rewrite already shared history to hide an ordinary correction.

The route project is Task Ledger: first keep a reproducible source history, then expose its data through a CLI and HTTP boundary, persist it in SQL, diagnose failures and prepare a release. This lesson owns one contract in that project. Run the worked example before changing the starter and explain which input makes the tempting shortcut fail.

Terminal practice: Use git log, git show <full-commit>:src/main.rs, then git restore --source <full-commit> -- src/main.rs and inspect the preview.

The compiler lab is independent of the reading question. Edit solution.rs; the app supplies a separate caller with normal, empty and adversarial inputs. A successful unchanged demonstration does not prove your implementation. After the lab, apply the same contract to the route companion project. Its README separates the on-device adapter from the desktop Cargo/TCP profile.
writing.exampleCaption: The worked implementation exercises restore narrowly from a known revision. Its tests demonstrate the stated finite contract.
writing.task: Return the current tree with exactly one path restored from a historical tree. Absence in history removes that path. Keep the public signature. Open the compiler lab and edit solution.rs; do not edit the private verification caller.
writing.success: The separate caller accepts the changed solution and rejects unchanged TODO, a wrong implementation and a printed success message.
writing.question: After restoring one historical file, what happens to unrelated current edits?
answers: A restore rewrites every previous commit
All files should revert to the historical tree
writing.feedback: Replacing the entire tree loses unrelated edits and exceeds the requested recovery.

recall.question: You restore `a` from a historical commit in which `a` did not exist. What happens to the current `a` and to other edited files?
recall.answer: `a` is removed, because the restore makes that one path match the historical tree. Every other path, including unrelated uncommitted edits, is left as it is.

recall.question: Why preview a historical file by full commit identity rather than a branch name, and what should happen after the restore?
recall.answer: Branch names keep moving, while a full commit identity keeps the preview stable. The restored file is an uncommitted edit, so review and commit it as a new change rather than rewriting shared history.

depth.misconception: All files should revert to the historical tree
depth.correction: A one-file restore must preserve every unrelated current edit.
